I don't remember the last time I actually took a duster to my own rig. But in my defence, I only recently upgraded my motherboard and that required I remove pretty much everything out of my PC in the process of ripping out an old ASRock mobo I could no longer trust in favour of an Asus. So, that basic action meant that I had cleaned my PC by proxy in the past couple of months, though without actively cleaning it.

Which has me straddling both camps of PC Gamer reader, it seems. Because, while the biggest single majority of readers we polled can't remember when they last cleaned their PC, either, a healthy 45% of readers have actually given their rig a thorough once-over in just the past six months.

Now, I get that you have to change your bedding/towels/pants more often than that, but six months is but a mayfly's daydream in the life of your gaming PC. So, I applaud all of you taking rig maintenance so seriously.

This all came off the back of a recent weekly poll where we asked the question: When did you last dust/clean your gaming PC? Sure, over a quarter of you are living in filth, but I'm still proud of the rest of you.

When did you last dust/clean your gaming PC?

Along with the 26% who can't remember, there are another 14% of readers who haven't lifted a finger to dust their PC in over a year. Then there are the paragons of virtue, the children of the light, the 5% who cleaned their PC only that very day they saw the poll. Blessed ones.

But if you look at the numbers in total, we are a culture in balance. There's a healthy 45% of readers who have cleaned their machines in the past six months, and on the other side another 40% of readers who haven't touched their PC with a duster in over a year, with a 15% fulcrum in the middle who have spent time cleansing their rig in the past 12 months.

Equilibrium is everything, but where do you sit on the cleanliness teeter-totter? And how important is it to you?

#3859. Ubisoft and at least two other companies are interested in buying Arkane, according to new report

Arkane Studios, which spent the last several months in limbo following Xbox's decision to divest itself from the studio, has apparently received buyout offers from several bidders.

Arkane was recently given until December to find a buyer and avoid closure, an extension from the previous November deadline, thanks to union efforts. Now, according to a Bloomberg report, a few companies have offered to buy Arkane from Microsoft.

The report names French publisher Ubisoft among at least three companies currently in talks with Microsoft to acquire the French studio. No decision has been made, however. The report also said Xbox considered selling Arkane to its management.

Should any of these offers be accepted, it would mean saving Arkane from closure, potentially saving up to 217 jobs and allowing the team to finish Marvel's Blade, which recent reports suggested is nearing completion. Bloomberg, however, said the game is "expected to be released within the next year or two", so it may not be as close as we think.

Arkane is one of several studios Xbox divested itself from as part of CEO Asha Sharma's big plan to reset the business, which saw over 1,600 job cuts with a further 1,600 to be made by the end of the fiscal year.

Studio divestitures include Psychonauts studio Double Fine, South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games, and State of Decay studio Undead Labs - which have all managed to go independent. Hellblade developer Ninja Theory and Arkane had the biggest question marks hanging over them, with Ninja Theory's fate seemingly the most dire after failing to find a buyer.

Given the December deadline Arkane was granted, we're likely to learn the identity of the studio's new owner in the near future.

I'm not the only one tickled by seeing these two cutting up while shooting the most recent Spider-Man movie. Fans sounded off in the comments section on both Instagram and Twitter, with some of the responses reading:

Clearly fans agree with me, and love seeing this real-life friendship, and the ways that it runs parallel to the dynamic shared between Peter Parker and Frank Castle. I'm personally hoping that we get to see more bloopers from Bernthal and Holland, who also got to appear in Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey earlier this year.

Given that Frank is one of the few friends that Spidey has after No Way Home's ending erased him from the world's memories, I hope we get to see these two characters get more scenes together in future MCU projects. I assume Bernthal and Holland would agree given their A+ friendship.

Spider-Man: Brand New Day is available to rent or purchase digitally as part of the 2026 movie release list, while the rest of the franchise is streaming over on Disney+. Fingers crossed we get more bloopers sometime soon.

#3855. Guild Wars gets its first major gameplay update in almost 20 years

ArenaNet and co-dev studio 2Weeks have announced Guild Wars Afterlife - the first major update for the game in nearly 20 years.

Coming to PC and mobile, Afterlife will add a new dynamic dungeon that'll morph after each run, and a skill-drafting system that'll allow you to create a distinct skill bar that'll change each time you take it on. There'll also of course be a new narrative to dig into, as players find new characters to interact with, and the new region of Xotecha to explore.

Afterlife is set to release on the 13th January next year, and will retail for $29.99 / €29.99 / £25.99. However, if you pre-order it between now and the 13th January, you can get it at a 20 percent discount.

This is a pretty big deal: the last time Guild Wars 1 got a massive injection of new stuff to dive into was back in August 2007 with the Eye of the North expansion. Following this, ArenaNet would move on to focus on Guild Wars 2 for the most part, leaving Guild Wars 1 servers up and running during that time.

However, the game has itself entered something of an afterlife following almost two decades of inaction. ArenaNet released Guild Wars Reforged - an enhanced upgrade to the original MMO - late last year. It also received a new dungeon in April, which has enticed new and returning players to dive back in.

Afterlife's reveal comes as ArenaNet is juggling development on three live service games at once. You've got Guild Wars Reforged (with Afterlife) of course, the more traditional MMORPG Guild Wars 2, and the highly-anticipated action-oriented Guild Wars 3. All will receive updates and support simultaneously, a sign of confidence in the health of the MMO space.

Michael Ilesanmi is having a blast on 90 Day: Hunt For Love, even if there's some drama headed his way. It wouldn't have been possible had he not finalized his divorce from Angela Deem, who hasn't been with the franchise since their split. Is she tuning in to watch her ex? I'm not sure, but she dropped a cryptic analogy when it came to her former husband.

Angela recently posted on Reels, calling out the various DMs she's gotten from people asking her if she's watching 90 Day content. She wouldn't specify what, exactly, but based on context clues from how she responded, people wanted to know if she was watching Michael on Hunt For Love. Here's what she had to say:

Am I watching that? No, what I can tell you what I am 'watching' and what I do know from being my age is - Watching a lot of horse races. I come from a, father that owned racehorses. When the horse jumps immediately first out the gate, he doesn't win, but the horse like we had that comes at the end to the front of the race wins. In other words, the first horse out of the gate ain't always the winner, but the last one comes in first.

I'm not 100% certain I get the analogy, but I think Angela is referring to the fact that Michael got back on the 2026 TV schedule before she did. She publicly claimed a while back that 90 Day Fiancé wouldn't want anything to do with him once they divorced, and I wouldn't be surprised if some fans reminded her of that when he was cast in Hunt For Love Season 2.

Angela continued with her analogy and was somewhat clearer. The gist seems to be that she's not watching Hunt For Love, but she is aware that Michael is back on TV. She may not have anything going on right now herself, but based on her closing comments, it appears she's of the belief that her time is coming:

Do you get my drift? So, no, I don't watch nothing that you're asking me. Why would I? No, but keep watching me because I'm that horse that's way behind that comes out the gate. I don't jump out the first when the gate opens. I come as it comes to the finish line. God bless Loyal Royals, and if you don't know the meaning of what I'm saying, then you're not in connect with me.

It's been two years since Angela Deem was last on 90 Day Fiancé, and so far, there's no word of her making a comeback. Back when the storyline involving her and Michael's split first aired, Deem said she was done, but she has bounced back and forth on whether she's actually done with reality television.

Meanwhile, on Hunt For Love, Michael seems to be starting a promising romance with Kay. Unfortunately, I think there's a chance it all falls apart once she hears about him spending a night with Brittany, even though he insists nothing is going on between them. It's a shame Angela isn't watching, because I would love to hear what she thinks about that.

Of course, 90 Day Fiancé has gone years without showcasing individuals, so I don't think it's impossible that Angela will come back. It really just depends on whether her popularity outweighs some of the wild antics she got up to on the show, and how viewers may feel about seeing her again.

90 Day: Hunt For Love airs on TLC on Mondays at 8:00 p.m. ET, and is on streaming for those with an HBO Max subscription. Those who skipped out on watching should catch up, because I'm loving this season a lot more than I did the first one!

#3852. Which WoW Forever ruleset to pick (and can you change later?)

Instead of realms, you just choose a ruleset to play. It's a pretty way of saying "playstyle" - and World of Warcraft: Forever likes things pretty.

World of Warcraft: Forever opens your latest journey to Azeroth with a big first step, as logging in for the first time gives you a choice of rulesets. No sign of the ages-old realmlist, just one choice of four (soon five). In theory, this choice should be simple – but somehow it’s still a headscratcher. It’s like the stakes got bigger, somehow.

So there’s Normal, PvP, Roleplay, and Roleplay-PvP. The first two you’re already familiar with. And if you’re not used to seeing roleplay servers, this can be quite new (but it’s what the “RP” in MMORPG stands for). Is there a difference in the choices, though?

As it turns out, not a lot. But they’re significant.

As the name implies, the Normal ruleset is for anyone who wants to log into WoW: Forever after a busy workday and do whatever. Maybe you want to grind to a certain level, do a couple of raids, or just walk around Dalamar (the lighting is amazing now, thanks to visual upgrades).

If you’re playing WoW for the first time, or if you’re not really into PvP, you can choose Normal. For MMO vets, you’d recognize Normal as the standard-fare “PvE” default mode. This is where we think a huge portion of players will be during launch, and maybe even afterward.

PvP is available but at your discretion. It’s a separate setting you have to enable, and it only applies in Contested or Enemy Zones.

Adventuring around Azeroth is fun, but what if you want to test your build against other players? What if you’re a Horde player and you meet some punk from Stormwind? There’s no need to resist going berserk in PvP, because duels are actively encouraged here.

PvP is automatically enabled here, and there’s no going back. You’re always open to attack in Contested and Enemy Zones. There are also some new rules:

The main ethos behind the transition from Warcraft 3 into World of Warcraft was always living inside Azeroth. What if you lived as a character who just started a life of adventure after the Third War?

With the Roleplay ruleset, you do exactly that. If you’ve always imagined acting out your character and immersing yourself in Azeroth, this is the ruleset for you.

Roleplay gives a massive “space” for players who love the idea of playing their own characters (r/WoWRolePlay has been up since 2012, for instance). Its naming conventions are stricter (no puns, please) and players are expected to behave a certain way (mostly roleplay).

If you want to kick things up a notch, there’s Roleplay PvP. It’s similar to Roleplay, except PvP is actively encouraged. Expect a lot of drama and grief (both the emotion and being maliciously killed in the game) from the other faction.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

There’s also a fifth “wildcard” ruleset that has yet to arrive in WoW: Forever, and that’s Hardcore.

As the name implies, Hardcore is for players who want a no-handholding experience. Naturally, Blizzard ups the ante for this challenge mode. It’s one strike, and you’re out.

But here’s what the difficulty mode means for the character specifically:

Unlike realms where each choice reveals a population density that preferred a “general type” of gameplay, rulesets in WoW: Forever have put a big emphasis on playstyle.

Remember, players in one ruleset likely enjoy and want to facilitate a specific playstyle. If you’ve gotten used to other players being in character in Roleplay, then Normal or PvP will be a jarring transition.

To avoid any conflict there, Blizzard put its foot down: no transfers between rulesets. If you want to play in another ruleset, you make a totally new character.

Likewise, you can’t play across rulesets. You’ll have to hop onto an alt in a different ruleset, say PvP, to play with your other friends in PvP. Same goes for the others.

Blizzard named one exception, and that’s Battlegrounds, which might include characters from different rulesets. No Hardcore, though.

There’s another catch, if “catch” was spelled “your name.”

When Blizzard introduced WoW: Forever, it also came with a big proposal: forging your legacy. Characters now come with first and second names, and no one else can have the exact two-name combination you picked for your character.

The idea is that, if you do something historic, everyone will know for sure that’s your character. Lore-wise, it also establishes a family name your future characters could use.

Naturally, this “exclusivity” component came with an early name reservation event between October 27 and November 3, 2026.

The big deal is that your choice of name is hard-set across all rulesets. That one name you picked in Normal can’t be used in PvP, Roleplay, and Roleplay-PvP.

If you’re not into roleplay, you’re good. But if you want a casual WoW experience and really sink your teeth into being an adventurer in Azeroth, well, that’s a tough choice.

Rulesets finally offer cleaner, much simpler choices for how to go about the World of Warcraft experience. At the end of the day, realms were only really important for two things:

If you don’t like fighting other players, stay away from PVP. Then high-population realms mean more chances of securing raid members all the time.

Now Forever makes this more intentional. Your playstyle takes precedence, and Blizzard handles everything else. So pick that ruleset and start grinding. Azeroth awaits.

Blizzard released World of Warcraft: Forever on November 4, 2026, for PC and macOS.

#3851. Dragon's Dogma 2 gets a timed collaboration with beloved anime and manga series Delicious in Dungeon, and it's out right now on PC, PlayStation and Xbox

Have you ever seen - or read - the wonderful Dungeon Meshi (known in English as 'Delicious in Dungeon')? It's a phenomenal manga series written and illustrated by Ryoko Kui, which was adapted into an anime series produced by Trigger in 2024. Long story short, it's about a group of adventurers in a fantasy world who lose an encounter with a dragon - who eats one of the party. What follows is a quest to revive the fallen party member (who happens to be the sister of one of the main characters), with the adventuring party learning to cook and eat monsters in dungeons as they uncover the stranger truth behind the world they inhabit.

If you can't tell, I think it's excellent, and the wait for the next season - landing in October 2027 - is practically killing me. It combines two of my biggest loves, cooking and fantasy, in a melting pot of a world that is intricately crafted and a story that is well-told. So imagine my surprise when I saw that Capcom announced a Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen x Delicious in Dungeon collaboration… and that it is live literally right now on PS5, Xbox, and PC platforms, coming in with a new update to the game.

"New allies and equipment are coming to the world of Dragon’s Dogma 2: Dark Arisen with the arrival of Official Pawns and special collaboration outfits inspired by Delicious in Dungeon characters Laios and Marcille," reads a press release from the publisher. "Delicious in Dungeon is a hit manga series created by Ryoko Kui that follows the adventurer Laios and his party as they venture deep into a dungeon, cooking and eating the monsters they encounter along the way. These iconic characters collide with the classic fantasy world of Dragon's Dogma 2: Dark Arisen in a limited-time collaboration that arrives today for PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, and PC."

For those playing on the newly-released Nintendo Switch 2 version of the game, this update will become available on Wednesday, 11th November.

Official Pawns modeled after the heavily-armored Laios and the elven mage Marcille can be recruited from the Riftstones, but there's a catch: these Pawns will only be available until Thursday, 28th January, 2027 on all platforms. So we've got a few months to play with them, but these helpful characters will not be permanent.

Additionally, players that load their data for Dragon's Dogma 2 during the collaboration period will receive special crossover outfits modeled after the attire of Laios and Marcille. These collaboration outfits will automatically be added to in-game storage and can be equipped by both the Arisen and Pawns. Once redeemed, these outfits will remain available even after the collaboration event ends.

The Skull Mask, the Spooky Mask, the Bunny Hood, and more are part of the Happy Mask Shop quest in OOT Remake

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Happy Mask Shop in Zelda Ocarina of Time has you run around Hyrule trading masks with characters for Rupees, including the Skull Mask, Spooky Mask, Bunny Hood, and the Keaton mask. Though these masks only serve as commodities to be traded with specific characters, if you can allocate all four to the right characters and complete this OOT quest, the Happy Mask Shop will give you access to four new masks that all have a very specific utility. Below I'll show you how to hand out all the Masks and the specific locations you need to look.

Keep in mind that the Switch 2 version is the same as the original, in that the Happy Mask Shop won't open in The Legend of Zelda Ocarina of Time until you open the passage to the Goron City. Fortunately, the guard who opens the passage will actually tell you that the Mask Shop is now open, flagging that you can start this questline.

Bought from the Mask Shop for 10 Rupees, you need to give this to the Guard in Kakariko Village who opens the passage for you, the same one who lets you know that the Mask Shop is open. He'll give you 15 Rupees in return.

Bought for 20 Rupees, head back to the starting area of Kokiri Village, where you start off and get the first Shield and Sword in Zelda Ocarina of Time, and turn North into the Lost Woods.

The moment you enter, head left through the hollow trunk to meet The Skull Kid, playing a tune on top of a log. He, understandably, will offer to take the Skull Mask from you, though only pay you ten for it. Cheapskate.

After buying the Spooky Mask for 30 Rupees, head back to Kakariko Village, and this time take the East exit to the Graveyard, but do so during daytime. Here you'll find a boy wandering around. Speak to him to give him the Spooky Mask, for which he'll give you 30 Rupees back.

The final mask in this sequence is bought for 50 Rupees. You can only sell it once you've progressed to the point where you have obtained the Three Spiritual Stones in the main story.

Sign up to our Switch 2 Spotlight newsletter to make sure you get the very latest news on Nintendo's new console and its games every week

Once this happens, head to Hyrule Field. There'll be a man who runs in circles around the field, practicing his running. If you go during the night, he'll be sitting beside the road and you won't have to keep pace. Either way, if you give him the Bunny Hood, he will entirely fill your wallet with Rupees, so it's a good idea to have expanded it as much as possible prior to the trade to really capitalize on that.

Having given these masks out, the Happy Mask Shop will now have four new masks in store that you can get, all of which serve a particular function. Here's what they do:

It's really only the Mask of Truth that provides the major advantage to gameplay, though some of the dialogue options and reactions from NPCs can prompt interesting lore information. Likewise, the cash infusion delivered by the Bunny Hood NPC can make Link incredibly rich, a great reward in and of itself.

Feel gud, not git gud; Phantom Blade Zero's action stands out for the ways it sheds the Souls and Sekiro formulas.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

What is it A martial arts action epicRelease date October 28, 2026Expect to pay £49.99/$59.99Publisher S-GameDeveloper S-GameReviewed on Intel Core i5 12400F, Radeon RX 6800 XT, 32GB RAM,Multiplayer NoSteam Deck UnsupportedLink Steam

Ever since I started Phantom Blade Zero, I've had a scene from Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon playing on repeat in my head. It's the sequence when Jen and Shu Lien face-off against each other in the martial arts hall. Jen is wielding the Green Destiny, a sword which can seemingly slice through all other weapons, but as it does, Shu Lien adapts.

She uses blades, spears, hook swords, a metal club, but every weapon she picks up, she immediately wields with martial prowess—it might be a bit of a wuxia trope, but it can't help but encapsulate the experience of playing Phantom Blade Zero. The protagonist, Soul's old comrade, Lei Dang, echoes this sentiment when you meet him: "You truly are a martial prodigy - you can master anything you learn."

In a crowded market of action games often borrowing more from Souls and Sekiro than they rightly should, Phantom Blade Zero sheds these strictures in favour of a martial arts adventure that's more about feeling good than getting good. It's not just the endless array of weapons and Phantom Edges (essentially Sekiro's Shinobi Tools) that Soul wields with effortless martial grace, it's about how the game makes you feel like a master.

Phantom Blade Zero managed to convince me—a Dark Souls veteran with 860 hours in Elden Ring—that perhaps you don't have to struggle against bosses to make them meaningful. Maybe a fight or two is enough when a game is packed full of incredible boss battles, each encounter feels great, and the experience is epic enough to satisfy you that you've seen everything it had to show.

Phantom Blade Zero is really a game for those who revel in action combat and its spectacle, but that's not to say it's super easy—it just has a way of making you feel like you're better than you probably are. During one fight with a drunken swordmaster and his flying blade, I parried and Soul dropped onto his back, grabbed the blade between his feet, then forward flipped, hurling the sword back at the boss. I literally pressed one button to do this.

Not to say it's super easy—it just has a way of making you feel like you're better than you probably are.

There are so many jaw-dropping moments—elaborate parries and executions, or dynamic attacks where Soul automatically engages an entire group of enemies—that basically had me yelling at the screen because I couldn't believe what I'd just pulled off. Like any good kung-fu movie, it's effortlessly stylish, but rather than the all-too-familiar drudgery that can stem from Soulslikes crushing you into the dirt and making you feel your skill level, Phantom Blade Zero more often tries to uplift you, reveling in the roleplay fantasy of a martial master.

It also makes the wuxia genre feel approachable. I'd be the first to admit, even as a westerner relatively familiar with Chinese mythology, I struggled to understand what was happening in Black Myth Wukong a lot of time. By comparison, Phantom Blade is a classic revenge plot. Soul, a martially-gifted orphan of mysterious providence, now outlaw, travels to the town of Pangzhen to confront his sworn brother and betrayer, Zuo Shang, after they stabbed each other through the heart. His replacement, The Tainted Heart, only lasts 66 days, so he has to beat Zuo Shang to the prize, a rumoured artificial heart, hence the top difficulty's fun and loreful limitation of 66 lives.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Though its dialogue is a bit on the nose at times, Phantom Blade does a great job of gradually exposing its ill-fated characters, dark setting, and sorrowful story of martial sects grasping to harness unearthly powers. It also carries forward Black Myth Wukong's tendency to surprise you with cutscenes of different styles, including Chinese shadow puppetry.

Coupled with its dark story, it makes for a far dirtier version of wuxia.

It's most adept at teasing its bosses, though, by telling their stories through found notes and Memory Flower collectibles in each region, or via Dark Souls 3 opening-style cinematics. Coupled with its dark story, it makes for a far dirtier version of wuxia, channeling aspects of kung-fu and wild west cinema as we see roundtables of fated standoffs with tragic foes we're yet to face.

Phantom Blade Zero is demonstrably not a Soulslike—hell, it's even less of one than Black Myth Wukong was. Though it has the recognisable structure of bells (bonfires) and remnant echoes (souls), it does away with almost everything else, much to its benefit.

This makes for an action game with a lot more momentum. Rather than banging your head against the same boss ten times, you might fight three or more bosses in the same period—Phantom Blade clearly understands that the spectacle of boss battles is one of the core pillars of a great action game, so there are a lot of them with varied gimmicks.

The game also takes notes from Sekiro, but mechanically responds to two of its, arguably, most debated issues. Namely:

Attacking, deflecting, and parrying to break a boss's stamina in Phantom Blade doesn't give you a critical attack, but instead grants a period in which they can't block your assault. This encourages experimentation, and ultimately, allows you to style on a boss however you wish for the duration. Being aggressive, versus baiting out parries, is encouraged, since regular attacks don't consume stamina and without crits, you have to progressively deal damage to win the fight.

Familiarising yourself with Phantom Blade's massive array of Phantom Edges (the Shinobi Tool equivalent) is also incentivised, since they use a spark resource you get a set number of anytime you rest, but can also recoup through accessories and skills. I personally used the gigantic Dread Axe to smash opponents, and the Fire Meteor, a brazier of green flame on a chain that you kick around to ignite enemies. There are also shields, bows, throwing knives, cannons, guns, spike balls and chains, bashpoles, and even summon options, to name a few.

What's more, since weapons and Phantom Edges gain new abilities every five levels, (up to 30), and Phantom Blade is extremely generous with upgrade materials, letting you easily refund everything you put into them, you're always experimenting. I feel like it says something that I upgraded four weapons and two Phantom Edges fully in my playthrough, yet still had 3 million remnant echoes and the means to level far more.

Good thing, too, considering I have another 20 weapons and 22 Phantom Edges to master in my New Game+ run.

I only have one chief complaint with Phantom Blade Zero. Though the game is quite large—it took me 50ish hours to do everything and unlock the "true" ending—it's unfortunately rather hand-holdy when it comes to its secrets, meticulously guiding you through the game with an almost exhausting quantity of quests and map markers.

It's unfortunately rather hand-holdy when it comes to its secrets.

Since Phantom Edges can be used to unlock areas in previous regions, it has some Metroidvania qualities, but none of these secrets feel especially significant, or equivalent to, say, what other examples of the genre have accomplished, like finding a secret region or boss in Silksong.

Despite appearances, the game is rather linear due to its quests, map markers, and where it places important progression items. Even its more secret, optional regions, are basically impossible to miss, which is such a shame when the game has multiple endings based upon where you go and what you do. It's a level of handholding that made me fervently wish Phantom Blade had taken more influence from Souls in this department at least, especially as playing regular difficulty sets up New Game+ and its escalating challenge in a really attractive way.

I'm rarely a New Game+ person, but upon finishing Phantom Blade, I immediately started again. The game lets you keep your weapons, Phantom Edges, and accessories, so you have more methods to deal with the now-tougher bosses you encounter earlier in the game.

Still, that alone is not enough to ultimately dampen my sincere enjoyment of Phantom Blade. It's a veritable feast for any lover of action combat and fun boss battles. Its soundtrack, too, is noteworthy, blurring the line between traditional Chinese folk music and modern genres in a way that really compliments the spectacle of every fight. I especially enjoyed the Banyan Tree theme, Asura of Wrath—who doesn't love a bit of throat singing?

The game also runs very well. My relatively humble RX 6800 XT produced decent results. Though I did get some more notable frame dips in certain fights with lots of particle effects going on, such as during heavier rain. But on the whole I am incredibly impressed with Phantom Blade Zero. I enjoyed it significantly more than Black Myth Wukong. Alongside Onimusha, it's definitely one of this year's must-plays for fans of action combat.

Feel gud, not git gud; Phantom Blade Zero's action stands out for the ways it sheds the Souls and Sekiro formulas.

#3848. Nexus Mods introduces new AI disclosure rules, but won't ban AI mods outright

"We hope what we have planned for now is a good first step."

Nexus Mods, the largest website for finding and downloading PC mods, has revealed new guidelines aimed at properly identifying mods created entirely using gen-AI or those created with AI assistance.

In a new blog post, Nexus clarified its stance on a number of topics, but said it won't ban AI-generated mods altogether. Going forward, mod authors are required to disclose whether or not their mods used AI, and clarify how it was used. A toggle has also been added, giving visitors of the site the ability to filter out any mods that use AI.

Aware of how controversial the decision not to have a blanket AI ban would be, site co-owner Foledinho explained that although "we are pro-human creativity", it would be "difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable".

"An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use," Foledinho explained. "We'd prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform."

That same courtesy extends to mods created entirely using AI, so long as that fact is disclosed. "This doesn't mean that any work done using AI will get removed; AI-generated mods are welcome on our platform provided that they meet certain criteria regarding permissions, transparency, presentation, and conduct," the post continues.

The new, mandatory disclosures cover existing mods, too, whose authors have 60 days to review whether their mods meet the new requirements. The new rules come alongside updates to the site's UI, which should make AI tags on mod pages more prominent. Not all backend changes will arrive at once, however.

"While we hope these changes will encourage everyone to disclose their AI usage, to be honest, that's not going to happen," Foledinho added. "Additionally, we are putting clear moderation standards in place, enforced with consequences for breaking the rules."

A different (albeit related) problem the deluge of AI-assisted mods introduced is the idea of remixing and modifying other authors' mods, often without their permission.

Nexus Mods doesn't have a solution for that problem at the moment, but the site is "working on introducing new permission options covering AI usage and training, as well as forks and derivative mods." By the same token, the post clarified the site won't itself use mods to train AI, or sell or license the mods to "anyone doing so".

This could prove to be a more complex problem to solve, given how often one mod relies on another mod to function, and that's saying nothing of contributions from other authors or users themselves.

Then there's the issue of AI-generated and AI-assisted thumbnails, which run the gamut from those entirely created by gen-AI to original shots upscaled or enhanced using AI tools. The post said no new rules governing those cases are being introduced, calling them "grey zones", but that "this discussion is not over yet."

"I'll be honest with you all, there are some details we still need to figure out and work through, especially when it comes to existing licences, forks, and how permissions apply to different versions of a mod," the post goes on. "But we want to get this right, and not rush through changes that could cause more problems further down the line. This does mean that these improvements will take longer to deliver, but we hope what we have planned for now is a good first step, and you'll bear with us whilst we continue to move in the right direction."

Just yesterday, indie game website itch.io was forced to expand its AI disclosure filter as 'AI slop' threatened to overwhelm the site. Previously, Valve came under pressure due to a perceived lack of curation around AI-developed titles during the most recent Steam Next Fest, prompting public outcry and a demand for more action from the company.

Tom Cruise is greatly known for two things. One of those is his sheer love for movies, and the other is his ability to perform massive stunts in order to entertain the masses. As a result, Cruise has put himself through the wringer, injuring his foot and breaking his ankle while working on the Mission: Impossible franchise alone. While the A-lister didn’t have to perform any major stunts for his 2026 movie release, Digger, he did have a physician on set. And we now know that due to details about co-star John Goodman’s wild injury.

Over a year ago, it was reported that the incomparable Goodman hurt himself while shooting Alejandro Iñárritu’s latest film. At the time, it was said that the Roseanne alum had suffered a hip injury and that he was doing fine. Goodman is now sharing his personal perspective on what happened that day on set, and the beloved actor’s take honestly sounds brutal. Nevertheless, he apparently had some serious support, thanks to Cruise’s crew:

I was stupidly wearing stockinged feet, no shoes. I went past Tom, my feet slid out and I went down parallel on my left hip. Tom’s physician was on set and one of his best friends is an osteopath, so I was operated on the next morning.

While it was unfortunate that Goodman ended up hurting himself while on set, he apparently got the support he needed right away, thanks to Cruise’s people. Many of Cruise’s co-stars have talked about how he’s had their backs at one point or another, and we can now add Goodman to that list. At the time, Goodman’s situation led to a delay in filming, and he recently explained that he had to do rehab in London for two weeks. As he recalled to The Times:

In a medical facility. Actually, an old-age home. Yeah. Then I went home and hit it every day, physically pushed it and got it done.

The film sees John Goodman play the role of Compson, the eccentric and easily influenced President of the United States who leans on Tom Cruise’s Digger Rockwell for guidance. As Goodman said during his interview, he “had a ball” working with Cruise, who went method to portray the film’s titular character. This makes just another instance in which Goodman has spoken highly of his time working on Iñárritu’s movie, and they came in the aftermath of polarizing reviews.

Early reactions to Digger were mixed, and that continued to be the case when full critic reviews began to be posted. The movie earned Tom Cruise his lowest Rotten Tomatoes score in almost a decade, and it holds a 52% critics’ score on RT, as of this writing. It does, however, hold a 77% audience rating on the aforementioned site as well. The movie did, however, flop at the box office and has amassed $49 million worldwide against a reported production budget between $125–180 million.

John Goodman shared his belief that reviews and bad buzz “killed” the movie before it even hit theaters. Still, it’s evident that even after the reactions and on-set injury, he’s still proud of the work, and Tom Cruise appreciates his collaborators’ efforts as well. As for me, I just appreciate that Cruise has medical staff on hand to tend to his colleagues’ needs.

Digger is still playing, so head to your local cinema if you’d like to check it out.

#3845. Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell loses his race for a seat in the US House of Representatives

Halo and Destiny composer Marty O'Donnell's political aspirations have hit a roadblock following last night's US mid-term elections. O'Donnell was campaigning for a seat in the US House of Representatives, running as a Republican candidate in Nevada's Third Congressional District, but is projected to lose.

The Associated Press called the race at 9am this morning, with incumbent Democrat Susie Lee currently holding 59.1 percent of the vote as of writing. O'Donnell currently has 38.6 percent of the vote, making a deficit of over 51,000 votes. The Associated Press estimates 86 percent of the vote has been counted, which if accurate, would make O'Donnell's comeback impossible. Lee seems to have ridden the 'blue wave' that has seen a huge number of seats across US Congress and Senate flip over to the Democrats.

O'Donnell, who is perhaps still best known for his music work, composed many of developer Bungie's most beloved soundtracks, creating music for the likes of Halo, Destiny, Myth, and Oni. He entered the political arena following his firing by the studio in 2014. Since then, he's been a figure of some controversy, describing LGBTQA+ people as an "existential threat" alongside Marxism and Islamists. He has also spoken out against same-sex marriage equality, and his comments drew understandable scrutiny during his recent campaign.

Per his website, O'Donnell was campaigning on a platform of economic improvement, small business support, increased border security, and anti-corruption measures. He did not claim corporate Political Action Committee (PAC) money - a hot topic this election cycle - but did receive financial support from the Trump-tied Safety and Affordability Super PAC, which notably pulled $2m in funding last month.

Following his departure from Bungie, O'Donnell won a substantial settlement from the developer after claiming he was fired "without cause". In a related 2021 judgement, O'Donnell was found in contempt of court after uploading Destiny assets to his personal YouTube channel.

#3843. One of Nintendo's Switch and Switch 2 cartridge manufacturers is exiting the business, which could make physical games more expensive

Macronix, longtime Nintendo hardware partner and one of the main producers of ROM memory, has announced it's leaving the business. ROM chips are key components in Switch and Switch 2 cartridges.

Industry analyst David Gibson shared the news on X, which Macronix announced in its latest earnings call. The company plans to phase out ROM products entirely by the end of the third quarter of fiscal year 2026.

As it stands, ROM products represent just 5 percent of Macronix's business, going off its reported sales for the third quarter. This is down significantly from 26 percent just one year ago. As a result, Macronix is shifting manufacturing capacity to instead focus on NOR (flash) and eMMC memory chips.

It's worth noting that Macronix is not the only company Nintendo relies on for ROM memory. Nintendo also sources parts from Rohm Co. (Oki Semiconductor), but losing a key partner puts more pressure on the already strained supply, which could result in higher prices.

As Gibson pointed out, that could also push more publishers - including Nintendo - to ship their games as Game-Key Cards instead, which do not include physical cartridges, avoiding the extra cost.

Although not directly stated, this is likely another side effect of the ongoing, global AI-driven memory and storage crisis. On top of making many consumer products unaffordable for millions, causing the prices of game consoles to rise and putting GPUs out of reach for PC builders, the shortages have also caused major memory manufacturers to redirect their resources to business segments where demand is higher.

Nearly one year ago, Micron, one of the three largest memory manufacturers in the world, announced it's exiting the consumer memory business and shutting down its Crucial brand.

This could put more pressure on Nintendo, already one of the last holdouts continuing to invest in physical media, to raise prices of games even further or abandon cartridges. Just last month, Nintendo said it has no plans to ditch physical games, in the wake of rival Sony's decision to end disc manufacturing in 2028.

#3842. Everything you need to know about WoW Forever leveling

Grinding to Level 60 in WoW: Forever will feel painfully familiar, but Blizzard hopes it's not as painful as Classic's.

World of Warcraft: Forever welcomes everyone to Azeroth for the first time for, well, the third time. And anyone who’s built a career out of creating alts throughout Retail and in Classic would want to just go through the motions and get to Level 60 ASAP to enjoy all the new endgame features WoW: Forever has to offer.

But with Level 60 as the capstone, it’s not going to be as quick a ride compared to other WoW expansions. And if this is your first time dipping your toes into an intense MMO like WoW, here’s a quick lesson in leveling in Forever.

For an MMO that lets characters experience the highs of being Level 120 (back in Battle for Azeroth, at least), Level 60 for Forever feels awfully fast. Or the worse alternative, the mid-point grind will probably be horrifyingly slow.

“We did not change the experience curve,” Kris Zierhut, WoW: Forever‘s principal designer told Sean Keach of The Sun. “So what we’ve really done is just created a different path. The experience curve remains the same.”

Blizzard devs also highlighted this with similar metrics from the WoW: Forever Beta. The average leveling time from Level 1 to 20 in Classic is 20.4 hours, compared to 20.5 in the Forever Beta.

“The big intent is to get you into the world and keep you in it,” Josh Greenfield, WoW: Forever senior game designer, said in the WoW: Forever podcast. “Part of the game is to protect and nurture social experiences. We want to keep you in the world as much as possible.”

But what does this mean for the rest of the leveling experience?

Leveling in WoW: Forever is standard-fare RPG mechanics. You get XP by turning in quests, killing mobs, and discovering new areas. For monsters specifically, you get more XP by fighting higher-level mobs compared to lower-level ones.

From your starting zone, expect that quests will eventually get you to a nearby zone with mobs scaled to your general level.

Expect to encounter more lower-level mobs in starting zones to help get you up to speed. Then they get less and less the more you level up. Blizzard said they’ll squeeze in extra spawn rates during launch and will balance things out eventually.

Leveling can get confusing when other people get involved. If you’re in a high-population area, chances are there are a lot more people also farming the same mobs. This is where tagging comes in.

Basically, if you tag or attack the monster first, you get first dibs on the XP. The monster’s name turns gray for them, which means someone else is already actively engaging the monster.

Even if they kill the monster, you get the XP. The same works if you kill a mob someone already tagged; this time they get the XP instead of you.

If this seems too confusing, you can always just buddy up.

No adventurer is an island, and one of the M’s in MMORPG does stand for “multiplayer,” so WoW: Forever does incentivize group play. When you party up with other players, you share any XP you get from killing mobs.

At first glance, this seems counterintuitive since you can just earn more if you kill them solo. But the idea is that you can theoretically tackle more powerful mobs and earn even more XP just because you’re in a team.

Plus, you don’t share Quest XP, so it helps to tackle zones together as a unit.

Alternatively, instead of buddying up, just take turns getting first tag on a monster. Everyone else helps, but the tagger gets the XP. Then rotate.

But take note that the higher-level the “helper,” the less XP the tagger will get.

Professions are leveled separately. Basically, things you do that actively involve the Profession will earn XP for it. After reaching a certain level, you have to rank up your Profession via the Trainer in order to access more benefits and potential craftable items.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

One of the fastest ways to tackle quests in WoW: Forever is the ages-old strategy of doing it zone by zone. Blizzard built Azeroth in such a way that quests will have you naturally go from one area to the next until such a point that you can choose whichever common-leveled zones you want to spend time in.

With an add-on like Questie, you can have a rough estimate of the claimable quests in the zone you’re in and gauge your plan from there. The usual strategy is to accept all quests in one zone, do everything in the vicinity, then turn in everything at once. By the time a quest sends you to the next zone, that’s the sign it’s time to move on.

When you stay in a safe location like an inn, a city, or even with the Cozy Sleeping Bag, you’ll end up in something called a rested state. In here, you start to accumulate something called Rested XP.

This is a concept taken straight from Classic. You know you’re there when your XP bar becomes blue instead of purple. As long as you’re eligible for Rested XP, you gain double the XP from monster kills. This eligibility depends on a “stockpile” of XP you accumulate as you stay rested. Here are other things to consider:

Always set your Hearthstone in an inn. If you have to log out at any point, you’ll have accumulated some Rested XP by the time you come back.

Since Forever is in part a reimagining of the vanilla WoW launch, it’s no surprise vets will have a specific leveling approach in mind. It’s a ritual at that point, especially for those who have an alt for just about any situation.

But take note that part of Blizzard’s plan is to focus less on farming mobs and doing more quests.

“Moving a lot of that experience (leveling) off of just the kills and onto the quests really incentivizes you to do that (the quests) at least once,” Greenfield said on the WoW: Forever podcast.

This also goes for dungeons, where dungeon quests now give more XP while dungeon mobs give less. Prioritize clearing dungeon quests for the first time, as this is where the most XP gain happens.

Anyone who’s ever tried leveling a character in Classic will be intimately familiar with the dreaded Level 40 grind. It’s just a point in anyone’s adventuring career where quests are scarce, and there’s really no “logical” point of zoning progression.

Back in the day, your choices beyond the questlines would be bouncing to and from your preferred farming zones. Forever wants to solve this by adding a couple more regions (and theoretically, quests) to help with that grind:

These zones will be new additions to staple zones of this level, such as:

Logging into World of Warcraft: Forever to see a Level 60 cap might make it feel… lacking for some reason. Level 60 always felt like the midpoint to something else, not really a capstone digit.

It could have been the history. WoW: Forever is pegged as a reimagining of the 2004 Vanilla launch, which did have the Level 60 cap.

But then again, it only took two years before The Burning Crusade raised that to Level 70. Come 11 years later, Battle for Azeroth gave us a monumental peak of Level 120, then Shadowlands squished everything back to Level 60. Then Blizzard just couldn’t get its hands off the max level, so here we are at Midnight, a couple more expansions later, with a Level 90 cap.

Basically, it felt un-Blizzard for them to declare WoW: Forever to be strictly until Level 60. If they keep the promise, leveling will be more interesting if they follow through by introducing more routes for that midpoint grind. And if they somehow start pushing the meter again, none of us would be really surprised.

World of Warcraft: Forever is out right now for PC and macOS.

Spoilers ahead for the first four episodes of Hulu's The Mob.

Over the last few years The Traitors (which is streaming with a Peacock subscription) has become one of my favorite shows of all time. The Emmy-winning reality show is showing no signs of slowing down, and the studio behind it has given us another campy competition series with The Mob. I'm having a blast watching its first season on the air, but I'm seriously mad that two of my three favorite cast members are already gone.

The Traitors cast lists are full of reality TV legends, and a solid group was also assembled for The Mob. The first two episodes proved that Willam Belli is reality TV gold, and she is a big reason why I was so invested in the show. I was also excited to see both The Sopranos star Aida Turturro and Dancing with the Stars judge Bruno Tonioli in the show as well, but they unfortunately both got whacked in the 3rd and 4th episodes, respectively.

Willam is my favorite RuPaul's Drag Race queen, so I was always going to be watching The Mob with my Hulu subscription. Still, the cast announcement thrilled me thanks to seeing a bunch of other familiar faces. The fact that a Sopranos star was included seemed brilliant, and I was so ready to see what Janice herself, Aida Turturro, would bring to the table.

She might have only been in three full episodes, but the Emmy-nominated actress was wildly entertaining. Whether she was talking non-stop during the wine job or screaming for Romeo during Episode 3, I couldn't get enough. There was talk about her being voted as the new Don, which would have thrilled me. It's for this reason that I was doubly disappointed when Real Housewives of New Jersey star Joe Gorga whacked her at the top of Episode 4.

Before this heartbreak, Bruno from DWTS was similarly whacked by Joe at the top of Episode 3. Despite pledging allegiance to him as Don, Bruno's time on the show ended up being cut short. Considering what a soundbite machine he is, this feels like a real missed opportunity for the burgeoning reality competition series.

I'm watching Dancing with the Stars for the first time this season, so I was curious about how Tonioli would be different on a show like The Mob. I was surprised and delighted to see that there was basically no change in the dancer and TV personality. He was still dramatically waxing poetic, just as he does when offering critiques on DWTS. This cracked me up, which is why I was so miffed that he got eliminated.

Luckily for me, Willam Belli is still in the game, and has gotten envelopes in 3/4 of the missions so far. If she gets eliminated, I will be seriously angry, as that leaves mostly people I'm not familiar with... the exception being the truly iconic Debi Mazar.

New episodes of The Mob air Mondays on Hulu as part of the 2026 TV schedule. Fingers crossed that Willam stays safe from being whacked... or even becomes the new Don. I mean, imagine the looks she'd pull out!

#3840. The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel fans ponder split timelines, alternative histories, and more as story speculation runs wild following latest teaser

Following the release of yesterday's brief new The Elder Scrolls 6: Sentinel teaser trailer, story speculation is running rampant across communities dedicated to the fantasy series, with fans theorising everything from alternative histories to split timelines.

Yesterday's teaser - which arrived as part of Bethesda's 40th anniversary celebrations and comes amid devastating cuts across Xbox's first-party studios - was minimal. It opened with a shot of desert sand, before revealing the subtitle 'Sentinel' and ending with a quote from an unknown character. It's not much to go on, but is proving just enough to encourage discussion around what may be in store for Bethesda's next RPG.

And a good place to start is that quote. "The scroll offered only a shimmer, a veil thinly lifted to my eyes," it reads. "A future lost. A victory undone. Sands of time scattered by fate." All this is attributed to Yazar, Moth Priest of High Queen Iradne of Hammerfell, , but some fans think the accompanying date - 4E 206 - might be just as significant.

"[Sentinel] likely takes place five or more years after the start of Skyrim," hypothesised Reddit user 04nc1n9. "Hammerfell is a monarchy, it hasn't changed to any other political system after their imperial secession. The monarchy of Hammerfell has a Moth Priest on hand, even though the Moth Priests are generally an Imperial thing. Hammerfell's monarch has access to an Elder Scroll after the Elder Scrolls scattered."

This unexpected link between Moth Priests and Hammerfell's High Queen has created speculation of its own. One theory, combined with the proximity of Sentinel's story to that of Skyrim, has the Thalmor play a key role. "[It's] likely the Thalmor being the antagonists with so little time having passed," wrote user Jonesketi, "and with justifiable knowledge of how to cause great harm with the Elder Scrolls, [this] would've prompted [Hammerfell] to begin their own preparations. [The Thalmor are] also such a fitting antagonist since we didn't get to kick them down in Skyrim, which would offer catharsis if it came in Sentinel."

As for the quote itself, its vague wording has inspired some particularly out-there speculation. Some fans are looking back to previously vanquished forces in the series, in light of the phrase "a victory undone", and are theorising it might refer to a Dragon Break - an in-universe timeline split in which multiple events can all occur and simultaneously be true once the timelines reconverge. In previous games, Dragon Breaks have served as a handy explanation for the multiple endings.

Talk of "undone" events set user Wafelze's mind to the Numidium, a giant mechanical golem whose activation in The Elder Scrolls 2: Daggerfall caused its own Dragon Break. "With how important time is to Skyrim’s story," they speculated, "it wouldn’t surprise me if this story is about time being entirely broken."

"See, I'm thinking it has to do with the creation of Nirn and Lorkhan," wrote Potential Film 7140. "The Altmer hate Lorkhan and men see the creation of the world as a victory. The elves did not ... maybe they'll try to undo what created the divines so they can go back to their original ancestry. Wildly out-there take but that's what my brain tells me."

What's more, the theories around split timelines and the Thalmor have converged with thoughts of a possible 'Man in the High Castle'-style alternate history setting for Sentinel, unfolding in a version of the world where the Thalmor have power. "Maybe the Empire originally held together after Oblivion, and the Thalmor used some cheater Elder Scroll magic to rewrite history so that they dunked on the Empire," suggested Original League 6094. "Or if I recall, Hammerfell was doing a great job beating the Thalmor as of Skyrim. Maybe the version of events got overwritten and now Hammerfell is under Thalmor subjugation, and the Elder Scroll is giving her glimpses of the timeline where Hammerfell won."

Will these theories prove to be true? With the launch of Sentinel still reportedly years away, it could be some time before we find out. But if nothing else, this feverish story speculation suggests there's a major hunger among fans for information - any information - about Sentinel. And that's no real surprise. After all, yesterday's teaser was only the second official look at a game whose reveal has been dragging on for over eight years now.

I'm modding GTA 5 every day in a quest to either transform it into a PC version of GTA 6 or break it entirely. Come back tomorrow to find out what new horrible thing I've done to Rockstar's baby, or check out what I got up to earlier.

Today's article is about ParkourV, but it is also about the vast graveyard of mods I have hitherto infected Grand Theft Auto 5 with and which then did not work. Did you know I at some point tried to install some sort of dating mod? I'd forgotten, but then there it was, asking me precisely how I would like to rizz up a babe as I initiated a frontflip from the roof of an 80-storey building.

Why? Because to make ParkourV work, I had to update my installation of ScriptHookVDotNet, one of those fundamental building blocks of modding on GTA, a bit like the Skyrim Script Extender for Skyrim. So now we live in a world in which I am constantly hitting keys and accidentally reanimating the corpses of mods I had installed and written off months ago. That's the world we have now and we're just gonna keep living in it.

Anyway. Parkour. The thing is, you see, GTA 5 is not really designed for parkour. Franklin, Trevor and Mike don't have the points of articulation for it. Attempting to do flips, then, just sort of rotates your entire body below the diaphragm while your head and chest area remain bolt upright, rigid in such a way that you could feasibly fly a flag from your own thorax.

Which looks odd. Nevertheless, it is pretty fun to scoot and roll your way through Los Santos. At one point, I attempted a double frontflip in the middle of a part of the map that had been deleted for some reason. It didn't quite work out, and I ended up colliding with and possibly killing a man in a fursuit.

#3837. God of War Laufey delayed three months to May 2027, as Sony Santa Monica escapes a packed February

"We will make the most of each moment until then."

God of War Laufey has been delayed. Sony Santa Monica's PS5 exclusive is now dodging the crowded month of February and will instead come out on 20th May, 2027.

Developer Sony Santa Monica announced it's pushing back the upcoming action epic via a brief social media post. While the studio stopped short of giving a reason for the delay, it did say it's using the extra time to polish Faye's solo adventure.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen. We don't take for granted the trust placed in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans," the studio wrote.

"With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20th, 2027," the statement continued. "We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey is notably the first game in the famed PlayStation series to not star Kratos in the lead role. This time around, Faye takes the lead through a version of the afterlife that houses gods and deities from multiple mythologies - and it's bringing back the original series' faster combat, too.

Of course, Kratos will return in future God of War games (he also shows up here and there during Faye's romp), and whatever that next Kratos game becomes, it'll supposedly connect to the events of Laufey, according to the developer.

On the bright side, the delay might be good news for anyone worried about their impossibly large and ever expanding backlogs. February 2027 is already packed with really exciting games - from the Fable reboot and Persona 4 Revival to Metro 2039. Hopefully, Laufey's delay gives everyone more breathing room.

Roseanne Barr has made it clear that she hasn’t really been on speaking terms with her Roseanne co-stars since she was fired from the 2018 revival. More recently, the actress found herself engaged in a back-and-forth with one of her longtime scene partners, Michael Fishman. The viral exchange between the two sitcom veterans led to Barr dropping a total of 13 F-bombs. Now, Fishman is opening up about what his feelings on Barr are in the aftermath of the verbal skirmish.

In August, Fishman – who played D.J. Conner – opened up about receiving social media messages from users who defend Barr and join her in criticizing her collaborators for moving on to the spinoff series, The Conners, without her. Fishman said he’d historically sought to block out such comments and turn the other cheek though, this time, he expressed agreement with the claim that Barr holds racially biased views and that Roseanne was fairly canceled after her tweet about Valerie Jarrett.

Barr responded to her on-screen son’s comments during an appearance on the Can’t Be Censored, during which she argued that Fishman was a “brainwashed bigot.” While dropping expletives, the comedian also argued that Fishman exuded prejudice for not listening to the comments she’s made. Fishman later expressed his desire to move forward but, during an interview with E! News, the former child actor still expressed warm feelings towards Barr:

I loved Roseanne from the first moment I met her at the audition, and she and I bonded. And that just grew over the course of the show. I'm always going to love her. I’m always going to care about her.

Fishman and Barr originally worked together on the first nine seasons of Roseanne, which aired on ABC from 1988 to 1997 (and is available to stream with a Peacock subscription). The show then returned in 2018 for a nine-episode tenth season on the Alphabet Network, and the show had already been renewed ahead of Barr’s firing. In the aftermath, Barr heavily criticized co-star and series EP Sara Gilbert for not defending her. Fishman doesn’t agree with Barr’s views, but that doesn’t inhibit his feelings:

Look, what I'm going through in a public sense is something a lot of people are going through in the private sense, which is we all love our family members. It does not mean we agree all the time. And the truth about that is just because you don't agree, it doesn't mean you stop loving each other.

Barr recently spoke about promises that were allegedly broken after she signed off on the Roseanne spinoff. She gave the OK on the conditions that ABC execs would publicly say she was not a racist and that the crew of The Conners would know that she helped to retain their jobs. According to the She-Devil alum, “it was all a trick,” and she allegedly wasn’t given the due she was expecting.

Meanwhile, Michael Fishman has maintained a relatively low profile since being let go from The Conners (for unknown reasons) after Season 4. Fishman has still, however, continued to speak affectionately about the show’s impact, including its early LGBTQ representation. As for whether Roseanne Barr will respond to his latest comments about her, that remains to be seen.

#3835. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Navi actor reprises her role after 28 years, but it was a total accident due to Nintendo's blind auditions

For The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's shiny new remake, Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice - 28 years apart - to deliver Navi's infamous "Heys!" and "Listens!"

The Switch 2's Ocarina of Time makes a pretty substantial change to the N64's Ocarina of Time, released almost three decades prior. There's proper voice acting this time, of course - not just grunts and murmurs and hyahs. But even when retroactively adding new things, Nintendo wanted to ensure the remake's cast matched the original's pretty faithfully, so the developer held blind auditions that eventually paved the way for one actor to reprise their role during Link's adventure.

"We felt that if we were going to improve the graphics so dramatically, the cutscenes needed to be fully voiced to match," director HokWai Ng explained in the most recent Ask The Developer blog. "But at the same time, we knew we shouldn't mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original. Navi's "Listen!" is one example. Even someone who's never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may have heard it before. We absolutely didn't want to change anything as iconic as that."

To maintain the original's nostalgic sounds and voices, Nintendo held blind auditions with the goal of finding actors who could recreate the "feel of the original game."

Series director Eiji Aonuma recalls that the team wanted to choose actors "based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original." And, who woulda guessed? "As fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming."

The duo didn't outright name which character they're talking about, but fans have long been speculating that Kaori Mizuhashi might be reprising her role as Link's trusty fairy companion Navi - at least, in the Japanese language version. A leaked online video of the game's credits now also confirms that Mizuhashi is back almost three decades later. I suppose it only makes sense that the person who most closely resembles Navi is Navi.

Chris Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Last month we got news that Wing Commander 3, the FMV space-combat sim with perhaps the highest concentration of Mark Hamill in any videogame, would be getting a remaster. Producer Jim Vessella is heading up the project, and revealed it during a presentation at the Portland Retro Gaming Expo.

What he did not reveal, it turns out, is that five other Wing Commander games—plus Road Rash—would be getting their own dolled-up re-releases, and that they'd all be dropping on Steam, GOG, and the EA App today as part of a larger bundle of 25 "EA Classics". No, I don't know why you'd buy them on the EA App either. It takes all sorts to make a world.

Here's the full list of games that are dropping. Anything labelled "Anniversary Edition" is an updated, remastered version of the original game. Anything not labelled that is simply a re-release.

If you're a GOG user, the only new things on that storefront will be the remasters—GOG's had all the other classic games for yonks now, but on Steam it's a veritable deluge of hearty, classic stuff. Personally, I'll just be glad to have a copy of Theme Hospital where all my other games are. And if someone fancies turning on Workshop support for it and integrating CorsixTH, they won't hear any objections from me.

On the remaster front, EA pinky promises it hasn't mucked the games up. "Each Anniversary Edition preserves the original look, feel and creative intent of the game, with quality-of-life updates to support modern systems, controls, improve performance and make the titles more approachable without compromising their authenticity."

You know what? I'm inclined to believe it. Vessella, who's more or less become the face of EA's old-game preservation and restoration efforts, also had a big hand in the work on the Command and Conquer Remastered Collection, and that was rather excellent even without access to the source footage of those games' FMV cutscenes, which seems to not be an issue here.

EA says the remasters are the fruit of "the discovery of a physical media vault containing thousands of Betacam, VHS, and D1 tapes alongside other media assets", while "the digitization process recovered the supposedly lost Master FMV sequences for these seven legendary titles, which were meticulously re-edited to restore the over 1,500 cinematic scenes across these games".

#3833. Best way to grind Research Points in Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered has a fair number of things to unlock, and you’ll need plenty of Research Points. You get Research Points by just playing the game, but there’s an easy way to fast track the process.

Let’s find out the best way to grind Research Points in the remastered version.

The method I have mentioned there was present in the original version, but the grind was significantly easier. Remastered version has made things harder, but the core method remains the same.

Your first task is to unlock Kiryu from its research tree and pick the Survival mode. Then, pick Monster Island as the location and map to kickstart the process.

Shoot a rocket as soon as the match begins, and the AI will always block it. Then, get close to your enemy and grab them with the window that you have created. Once you grab the enemy, get close to the wall just behind the spot where the AI spawns.

You’ll find a lava pit at the location, and you can then use Kiryu’s fierce attack to launch the enemy over the wall without breaking it. Now, the enemy will take 10 damage per second due to the lava.

Once your main tasks is done, your next job is to keep them locked in the pit without failure. If they try to escape, grab and toss them in the lava once again.

When the enemy is in the pit, the wall will usually remain intact. However, the enemy can sometimes wall the hug and take no damage. If that happens, don’t break the wall yourself. Instead, bait them to do that task instead for you. Your only focus is to ensure that the enemy stays in the lava and keeps taking damage.

The Hunger Games movies were wildly popular during their original run, and Panem has returned to the big screen thanks to author Suzanne Collins' prequel novels. The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes did well in theaters, and we've got another book to screen adaptation coming this month with Sunrise on the Reaping. The movie stars actor Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy, the role famously originated by Woody Harrelson in the original series (which is streaming with a Hulu subscription). I asked both director Francis Lawrence and the cast about which character should get a prequel next, and their answers were solid.

Sunrise on the Reaping's reviews have been praising the way the the cast embodied younger versions of beloved characters, including Haymitch, Wiress, Beetee, and Mags. I want to see more prequels, and as you can see in the video, I asked Lawrence about which characters he'd like to see explored in this way. He told me:

There's so many amazing characters. We talk about Finnick would be a great one, Johanna Mason would be a great one. You know, Mags. I mean, even just go doing a weird one and going to The Dark Days and doing something completely different. She's talked about Plutarch would be an interesting one to explore. Just because his story is so fascinating, I think. So there's a lot of options, but we always wait for Suzanne.

As a day 1 fan of the Hunger Games franchise, I would absolutely watch any of these movies. Soon after Sunrise on the Reaping was announced, fans started campaigning to see a young Finnick movie. I also love Johanna Mason, who was played to perfection by Jena Malone in the final few movies of the OG series. Plutarch is also another great choice, especially considering how he was secretly fighting Snow from within the Capitol. Jesse Plemons plays him in the new movie, taking on the mantle from late actor Philip Seymour Hoffman.

Francis Lawrence also name-dropped Mags, who is played in Sunrise on the Reaping by the incredible Lili Taylor. When I posed the same prequel question to her, she offered another intriguing character who she'd like to see fleshed out in this way. In her words:

God, I know that's so, there's so many characters. I mean, maybe Beetee, maybe Beete.

Sign me up. Beetee was famously played by Jeffrey Wright in the original movies, an honor that goes to Kelvin Harrison Jr. in the new prequel. Having seen the movie early, I have to say he does an INCREDIBLE job in this role, with his voice sounding nearly identical to his predecessor. He's worked with Wright a few times before, which no doubt why the impression of his vocal cadence is so accurate.

In Sunrise on the Reaping Beetee is forced to serve as a mentor for the Quarter Quell, while his son Ampert is one of the District 3 tributes. This was done as a punishment for him rebelling against The Capitol, and I'd love to see both that event and his Hunger Games explored in a future book and/or movie.

As Francis Lawrence points out, what comes next is actually in the hands of Suzanne Collins. If/when she writes another prequel that would open the door for yet another film adaptation. Clearly Panem is full of compelling characters, many of which fans would like to see given their very own story.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping will arrive in theaters on November 20th as part of the 2026 movie release list. Bring your tissues, because it's a brutal Quarter Quell.

#3831. Arkane union says closing the studio "would probably be more expensive" for Xbox than simply finishing Marvel's Blade

"Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic."

Xbox would probably spend more money shutting down Arkane Lyon than it would trying to finish and release Marvel's Blade, according to a union representing workers from the beloved imsim studio.

In a statement posted to the STJV (Syndicat des travailleureuses du jeu vidéo) website, the French union claimed that development on Marvel's Blade is "going fine" and is shaping up to be on par with Arkane's widely acclaimed gameography. By choosing to part ways with and potentially close the famed studio, the union says Microsoft is "sabotaging the game it funded."

After Xbox's sweeping job cuts and divestments from several first-party studios, Arkane was recently given until December to find a new buyer and ensure its future. Ubisoft Entertainment (Assassin's Creed, Rainbow Six) is reportedly one of the companies interested in buying the studio behind Dishonored, Prey and the upcoming superhero adaptation, though nothing has been finalised yet.

The union also blamed many of the studio's problems on Microsoft - a hiring freeze that lasted more than a year supposedly inflated the game's budget and caused additional internal delays. "Microsoft now use those same delay and additional costs as a reason to close the studio," the statement said.

"Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," it continued. "The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft's short term financial goals[...] The decision to close Arkane is solely the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization. Arkane is profitable. Just not profitable for Microsoft."

The union's list of demands now asks for employees to be able to have a say in choosing a potential buyer, as well as protections against any layoffs that might happen in the next few years. Should acquisition talks fail, the union claimed that the resources in Microsoft's redundancy package are "outrageously low" - so it's also demanding a redundancy payment of €200,000 per employee and further support.

Arkane's not the only developer reeling from Xbox's cuts. Double Fine (Psychonauts), Compulsion Games (South of Midnight) and Undead Labs (State of Decay) all managed to buy their independence, but had to lay off some staff as a result. It's not looking good for Hellblade developer Ninja Theory, either.
